title: Emotional Health After Birth
learningGoals: Tell the baby blues from postpartum depression
Recognize postpartum anxiety and know that scary thoughts are common
Know that postpartum psychosis is an emergency
Know who's at higher risk, and that treatment works
Know where to get help right away, for you or a partner

review.notes: Drafted 2026-10-18 as lesson 6.4 of Module 6 (Postpartum Recovery, Mood, and Red Flags). Goes deeper than lesson 6.2's baby blues comparison and crisis slide; the crisis slide here repeats 6.2's wording and numbers on purpose. Builds on lesson 6.2 (blues or depression, thoughts of harm) and lesson 6.5 (rest and help at home). Sources were found by web search only; this session could not open the pages, so every new source needs to be opened and confirmed. For the reviewer: the baby blues being very common and passing within about 2 weeks matches lesson 6.2 and the ACOG FAQ in part; postpartum depression symptoms and about 1 in 8 follow the CDC symptoms page; onset most often 1 to 3 weeks and up to a year after birth, risk factors, and treatability follow the ACOG FAQ; anxiety being as common as depression, and unwanted intrusive thoughts being common and not acted on, are standard perinatal mental health teaching not found on ACOG or CDC patient pages; ACOG CPG 5 covers anxiety treatment; postpartum psychosis being rare, starting suddenly in the first weeks, its signs, emergency care, and higher risk with bipolar disorder follow ACOG CPG 5 and 4 in part, with the symptom list and 'don't leave them alone with the baby' as standard teaching; not stopping mental health medicines only because of pregnancy or breastfeeding follows ACOG CPG 5; many medicines being compatible with breastfeeding follows the AAP postpartum depression and breastfeeding page as described in search results; nearly everyone who gets treatment recovering follows the ACOG FAQ; mood screening at postpartum visits follows ACOG CPG 4, and screening at the baby's 1, 2, 4, and 6 month checkups follows the AAP policy news page; the Postpartum Support International helpline (1-800-944-4773, call or text) is listed on the ACOG FAQ, though PSI itself is not an approved organization; partners' depression follows the AAP partner page; the crisis slide's 988, 1-833-TLC-MAMA, and 911 follow the CDC resources page and match lesson 6.2, with 'call or text' for the hotline as listed by CDC.

slides.heading: Emotional Health After Birth
onScreen: Module 6: Postpartum Recovery, Mood, and Red Flags
slides.narration: Having a baby brings big feelings: joy, love, worry, and sometimes sadness, all mixed together, often on very little sleep. In this lesson, we'll cover the baby blues, postpartum depression and anxiety, a rare emergency called postpartum psychosis, who's at higher risk, how treatment helps, and how partners can be affected too. Mood changes after birth are common, they're not your fault, and help works.

visual.description: At home in soft morning light, a new parent sits by a window holding a mug, looking thoughtful but calm, while their partner sits beside them with a gentle hand on their shoulder; the newborn sleeps on their back in a bare bassinet nearby. Both adults in everyday clothes. No pregnant belly. Exactly one baby. No readable writing.

slides.heading: The baby blues
onScreen: Weepy, moody, worried, or overwhelmed in the first days
Very common, as hormones shift and sleep is short
Usually passes on its own within about 2 weeks
Rest, food, and help from others make a difference
slides.narration: In the first days after birth, many new parents feel weepy, moody, worried, or overwhelmed, sometimes all in the same hour. This is called the baby blues. It's very common, as hormone levels drop quickly after birth and sleep is short. The baby blues usually pass on their own within about two weeks. Rest when you can, eat regular meals, and let others help. Talking about how you feel helps, too. If the feelings last longer than two weeks, or feel too big, it may be something more, and it's time to tell your care team.

visual.description: Four simple icons with short labels: a droplet for weepy or moody, a moon for short sleep, a calendar for usually passes within 2 weeks, and a group of people for rest and help from others.

slides.heading: Postpartum depression
onScreen: Sad, empty, or hopeless most days; little joy in things you used to enjoy
Crying more than usual, anger, or feeling distant from your baby
Doubting you can care for your baby
Common, about 1 in 8, and can start any time in the first year
slides.narration: Postpartum depression is stronger and lasts longer than the baby blues. You might feel sad, empty, or hopeless most of the day, or lose interest in things you used to enjoy. You might cry more than usual, feel angry, feel distant from your baby, or doubt that you can take care of them. Sleep and appetite may change in ways that aren't just from caring for a newborn. Postpartum depression is common, affecting about one in eight people who give birth. It most often starts in the first few weeks, but it can begin any time in the first year. It's a health condition, not a weakness, and it can be treated.

visual.description: Four simple icons with short labels: a cloud for sad or hopeless most days, a heart for feeling distant from your baby, a circled question mark for doubting yourself, and a calendar for any time in the first year.

slides.heading: Anxiety and scary thoughts
onScreen: Worry that won't stop, racing thoughts, or panic
Trouble sleeping even when your baby sleeps
Unwanted, frightening thoughts about your baby getting hurt are common
Having these thoughts doesn't mean you'll act on them; tell your team
slides.narration: Anxiety after birth is as common as depression, and the two often come together. You might worry constantly, have racing thoughts or panic attacks, feel on edge, or be unable to sleep even when your baby is sleeping. Some parents have sudden, unwanted thoughts or images of their baby getting hurt, and may check on the baby again and again. These thoughts are common, they're upsetting precisely because you don't want them, and having them doesn't mean you'll act on them. Tell your care team; anxiety and these thoughts respond well to treatment.

visual.description: Four simple icons with short labels: a lightning bolt for racing worry or panic, a moon for trouble sleeping, a thought bubble for unwanted scary thoughts, and a phone for telling your team.

question.prompt: Four days after birth, you cry easily and feel overwhelmed, but you're also enjoying your baby. What's most likely?
options: The baby blues, which usually pass within about 2 weeks
A sign you'll never bond with your baby
question.explanation: Feeling weepy and overwhelmed in the first days is common and usually passes within about two weeks. If it lasts longer or feels too big, tell your care team.

slides.heading: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency
onScreen: Rare, usually in the first weeks after birth
Seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or believing things that aren't true
Confusion, not sleeping for days, or acting very differently
Call 911 or go to the emergency department right away
slides.narration: Postpartum psychosis is rare, but it's a medical emergency. It usually starts suddenly, in the first weeks after birth. Signs include seeing or hearing things that aren't there, believing things that aren't true, feeling confused, being unable to sleep for days, or acting very differently from usual. The person may not realize anything is wrong, so support people often notice first. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department right away, and don't leave them alone with the baby. With quick treatment, people recover. The risk is higher with a history of bipolar disorder, so tell your care team about that before birth.

slides.heading: Who's at higher risk
onScreen: Depression or anxiety before or during pregnancy, or after a past birth
Bipolar disorder, or a family history of mood conditions
Little support, or big stresses like money worries, loss, or a move
A hard pregnancy or birth, or a baby in the NICU
slides.narration: Anyone can have a mood or anxiety condition after birth, but some people are at higher risk. That includes people who've had depression or anxiety at any time, before, during, or after a pregnancy, and people with bipolar disorder or a family history of mood conditions. Having little support, or big stresses like money worries, a loss, or a move, raises the risk, and so can a hard pregnancy or birth, or a baby in the NICU. If any of these apply to you, tell your care team now, so you can plan ahead together. If you take medicine for your mental health, don't stop it without talking to your team.

visual.description: Four simple icons with short labels: a clipboard for past depression or anxiety, a family of people for family history, a house for big stresses, and a hospital for a hard birth or NICU stay.

slides.heading: Getting help works
onScreen: You'll be asked about your mood at checkups, yours and your baby's; answer honestly
Talk therapy, medicine, or both
Many medicines can be taken while breastfeeding; ask your team
Postpartum Support International: 1-800-944-4773, call or text
slides.narration: Your care team will ask about your mood at your postpartum visits, and your baby's doctor will ask at your baby's checkups in the first six months. Answer honestly; these questions are there to help you, not to judge you. Treatment works. It may include talk therapy, medicine, or both, and nearly everyone who gets treatment gets better. Many medicines for depression and anxiety can be taken while breastfeeding, so you don't have to choose between your health and feeding your baby; ask your team. Support groups help, too, and Postpartum Support International offers a free helpline at 1-800-944-4773, by call or text.

visual.description: A calm, bright clinic room: a new parent sits in a comfortable chair talking with a kind clinician who listens and takes notes on a clipboard with no readable writing; the parent's newborn sleeps in a car seat carrier on the floor beside them. Both adults in everyday clothes. No pregnant belly. Exactly one baby. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Partners and support people
onScreen: Partners can get depression and anxiety after a birth, too
Watch for changes in your loved one, and believe them
Help with nights, meals, and time to rest
Encourage care, and go with them if you can
slides.narration: Partners can have depression and anxiety after a baby arrives, too, and it can show up as irritability, pulling away, or working all the time. If that sounds like you, talk to your own doctor. Support people, you're often the first to notice a change. Watch for the signs we've covered, and if your loved one says they're struggling, believe them. Help in practical ways: take a night feed so they can sleep, bring meals, and protect time for rest. Encourage them to talk to their care team, and offer to go with them.

visual.description: Evening at home under soft lamp light: a partner in everyday clothes gives the newborn a bottle in an armchair while the new parent rests on the sofa nearby under a blanket, and the two smile at each other. Both adults fully clothed. No pregnant belly. Exactly one baby. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
onScreen: These thoughts need help right away
Call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), free, 24/7
In an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department
slides.narration: If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, you are not alone, and you deserve help right away. Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, at 1-833-TLC-MAMA, which is free, confidential, and open 24 hours a day, in English and Spanish. If you feel you might act on these thoughts, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Support people, if someone you love says something like this, stay with them and help them get care.

question.prompt: Your partner, two weeks after birth, hasn't slept in three days and says the TV is sending them messages about the baby. What should you do?
options: Let them rest and check again in the morning
Call 911 or go to the emergency department now, and stay with them
Schedule a visit at their next checkup
question.explanation: Not sleeping for days and believing things that aren't true can be signs of postpartum psychosis, a medical emergency. Get emergency care now, and don't leave them alone with the baby.

slides.heading: Your emotional health plan
onScreen: Anything in your history to share with your care team
Who you'll tell if you're struggling
Who will help you get rest in the first weeks
slides.narration: Let's make a plan. Is there anything in your history, like past depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder, that you'll share with your care team? Who will you tell if you're struggling? And who will help you get rest in the first weeks? Save your answers to your Birth Readiness Brief, along with the helpline numbers.
slides.prompt: Write anything in your history to share with your care team, who you'll tell if you're struggling, and who will help you rest in the first weeks.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Baby blues: common, and usually gone within about 2 weeks
Depression or anxiety: stronger, longer, any time in the first year, and treatable
Seeing or hearing things, or not sleeping for days: call 911
Thoughts of harm: 988 or 1-833-TLC-MAMA, any time
slides.narration: Let's recap. The baby blues are common and usually pass within about two weeks. Postpartum depression and anxiety are stronger, last longer, can start any time in the first year, and get better with treatment, including medicines that work with breastfeeding. Postpartum psychosis is rare but an emergency: call 911. And if you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, call or text 988 or 1-833-TLC-MAMA, any time. Partners can be affected too. Whatever you're feeling, you're not alone, and help works.

reviewQuiz.prompt: How long do the baby blues usually last?
reviewQuiz.explanation: The baby blues usually pass on their own within about two weeks. Feelings that last longer or feel too big may be postpartum depression or anxiety, so tell your care team.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which is true about treatment for postpartum depression?
options: You have to stop breastfeeding to take medicine
Therapy, medicine, or both work, and many medicines are fine while breastfeeding
It goes away on its own, so treatment isn't needed
reviewQuiz.explanation: Talk therapy, medicine, or both help, and many medicines can be taken while breastfeeding. Nearly everyone who gets treatment gets better.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Who can get depression after a baby is born?
options: Only the person who gave birth
Only people with a history of depression
The birthing parent and partners, too
reviewQuiz.explanation: Postpartum depression is common in people who give birth, and partners can be affected, too. Anyone who's struggling should talk to their doctor.
